title: Heat as a training tool for cool conditions
goal: Explain the idea of using heat to raise performance in cool air, the evidence for and against it, and how to judge such claims.

steps.title: The idea: heat as a training tool
steps.text:
The pitch is simple. Heat acclimation expands [plasma volume](g:plasma-volume) within days. If that lifts stroke volume and cardiac output, [VO₂max](g:vo2max) and performance might rise in cool air too [[c:hope]]. Over weeks, heat might also raise [haemoglobin mass](g:haemoglobin-mass) by making more red cells, a slow process called [red cell production](g:red-cell-production). More red cells carry more oxygen.

The two changes run on different clocks: plasma volume moves in days, haemoglobin mass in weeks. A heat block would have to be long enough for the second one.

The key word in a 2015 review of acclimation was 'potentially': it was a hypothesis, to be tested in cool air.

claims.text: Heat acclimation may improve aerobic performance in warm-hot environments and potentially in temperate environments.

evidence.quote: Exercise heat acclimation induces physiological adaptations that improve thermoregulation, attenuate physiological strain, reduce the risk of serious heat illness, and improve aerobic performance in warm-hot environments and potentially in temperate environments.

steps.title: The 2010 result
steps.text:
Twelve trained cyclists did 10 days of exercise at about 50% VO₂max in 40 °C. Eight matched controls did the same exercise at 13 °C. Both groups were tested in cool (13 °C) and hot (38 °C) air.

In cool air the heat group gained **5%** in VO₂max (66.8 to 70.2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹) and **6%** in time-trial work (879.8 to 934.7 kJ). Plasma volume rose 6.5% and maximal cardiac output 9.1%. The controls did not change [[c:lorenzo-result]].

The controls were matched, not randomised, and the groups were small, so one study could not settle it.

claims.text: After 10 days of heat acclimation, trained cyclists gained VO₂max and time-trial work in cool air; matched controls trained in cool air did not change.

evidence.quote: Heat acclimation increased VO2max by 5% in cool (66.8 ± 2.1 vs. 70.2 ± 2.3 ml·kg(-1)·min(-1), P = 0.004) and by 8% in hot (55.1 ± 2.5 vs. 59.6 ± 2.0 ml·kg(-1)·min(-1), P = 0.007) conditions.
Heat acclimation improved time-trial performance by 6% in cool (879.8 ± 48.5 vs. 934.7 ± 50.9 kJ, P = 0.005) and by 8% in hot (718.7 ± 42.3 vs. 776.2 ± 50.9 kJ, P = 0.014) conditions.
Heat acclimation increased plasma volume (6.5 ± 1.5%) and maximal cardiac output in cool and hot conditions (9.1 ± 3.4% and 4.5 ± 4.6%, respectively).

steps.title: Later trials: no clear gain in cool air
steps.text:
Later trials did not repeat it. Of 18 trained cyclists, 9 trained 2 weeks outdoors at about 35 °C and 9 in cool air. The heat group improved its time trial in heat by 16%, but VO₂max and outdoor time trial in cool air did not change [[c:karlsen-null]]. Seven men in a crossover study trained 10 days at 38 °C: plasma volume rose 6% and sweat sodium fell 19%, yet VO₂max and time trial at 18 °C were unchanged [[c:keiser-null]].

In 21 cyclists, 5.5 weeks of heat training (28 sessions) raised a cool 15 km time trial by 17 W. The cool-trained controls gained 17 W too [[c:mikkelsen-null]].

claims.text: Two weeks of outdoor heat training improved time trial in the heat but did not transfer to VO₂max or outdoor time trial in cool conditions.

evidence.quote: However, for the well-trained endurance athletes, this did not transfer to an improved aerobic exercise capacity or outdoor TT performance in cool conditions.

claims.text: After 10 days of heat training, VO₂max and time trial at 18 °C were unchanged, though plasma volume rose and sweat sodium fell.

evidence.quote: Following heat training both were increased in T38 (9.6 ± 2.1 and 10.4 ± 3.1%, respectively), whereas both V̇o2max and time trial performance remained unchanged in T18.

claims.text: In 5.5 weeks of heat training, a cool 15 km time trial improved by 17 W in both the heat group and the control group.

evidence.quote: TT performance tested in 14°C was improved for HEAT and average power output increased from 298 ± 6 to 315 ± 6 W (P < 0.05), but a similar improvement was observed for CON (from 294 ± 11 to 311 ± 10 W).
Based on the present findings, we conclude that training in the heat was not superior compared to normal (control) training for improving aerobic power or TT performance in cool conditions.

debate.question: Does training in the heat improve VO₂max or performance in cool conditions?

sides.position: Yes: a 10 day trial raised VO₂max by 5% and time-trial work by 6% in cool air, and a pooled analysis found a small average VO₂max gain (its abstract does not split cool and hot test conditions).
Not shown: three later trials of 10 days to 5.5 weeks found no gain in VO₂max or cool-air performance beyond what control training gave.

steps.title: Net effect: change in heat group minus change in control
steps.problem: In a trial, the heat group's cool 15 km time-trial power rose from 298 to 315 W, and the control group's from 294 to 311 W. What did heat training add?
steps: Both groups train, so both can improve. The effect of heat is the difference between the two changes.
Heat group change = 315 − 298 = 17 W. Control change = 311 − 294 = 17 W.
Reading only the heat group (+17 W, about 5.7%) would credit heat with a gain that the controls got anyway.

steps.title: Haemoglobin mass and plasma volume
steps.text:
Haemoglobin mass is the best-supported hope. In 21 cyclists after 5.5 weeks it rose 34 g with heat and 2 g with cool training; the group difference was not clear (p = 0.061), and plasma volume rose in both groups [[c:oberholzer]]. In 25 elite skiers, five weekly heat suit sessions gave 30 g more haemoglobin mass than controls, but no difference in VO₂max or a 15 min run [[c:ronnestad]]. Pooled data suggest each extra heat exposure adds about 1.9 g [[c:mcd-hb]].

Open questions: does a few grams of haemoglobin mass change performance, and how much of the plasma volume gain is just training?

claims.text: In 21 cyclists, haemoglobin mass rose 34 g with heat and 2 g with cool training (group difference unclear), and plasma volume rose in both groups.

evidence.quote: There was also a main effect of time (p = 0.038) for Hbmass with +34 ± 36 g in HEAT and +2 ± 33 g in CON and a tendency toward a higher increase in Hbmass in HEAT compared to CON (time × group interaction: p = 0.061).
PV increased (p = 0.004) in both groups, by 303 ± 345 ml in HEAT and 188 ± 286 ml in CON.

claims.text: Five weeks of heat suit training raised haemoglobin mass by 30 g more than control in elite skiers, without a detectable gain in endurance performance.

evidence.quote: HEAT induced a larger increase in Hbmass and red blood cell volume after five weeks with five weekly heat suit training sessions than CON, but with no detectable group differences on physiological determinants of endurance performance or actual endurance performance in elite CX skiers.

claims.text: Each additional heat acclimation exposure increased haemoglobin mass by about 1.9 g in a pooled analysis.

evidence.quote: An additional HA exposure increased hemoglobin mass (1.9 g [0.6, 3.2])

points: The idea: heat expands plasma volume in days and perhaps haemoglobin mass in weeks, which might lift VO₂max and performance in cool air.
A 2010 trial with matched controls found VO₂max up 5% and time-trial work up 6% in cool air; the groups were small and not randomised.
Later trials (2 to 5.5 weeks) found no clear gain in cool air; in one, the control group improved as much as the heat group.
Haemoglobin mass may rise with long or suit-based heat training (about 30 g in skiers), but no clear performance gain has been shown.
To judge a heat training claim, ask for a control group and look at the control's change too.

variants.stem: Which chain of effects is the hope behind heat training for cool-weather performance?

options.text: More plasma volume leads to more cardiac output, so VO₂max could rise
options.why: Right: the proposed route is a larger blood volume and stronger pumping.

options.text: More sweating leads to lighter body mass, so speed rises
options.why: Sweat loss is regained by drinking and is not the proposed route.

options.text: Heat makes muscle fibres switch from slow to fast type
options.why: Heat acclimation is not proposed to change fibre type.

options.text: Heat lowers resting heart rate, which is the same as fitness
options.why: A lower heart rate in the heat is an adaptation to heat, not fitness.

variants.stem: A coach wants to use heat blocks to raise a cyclist's cool-weather VO₂max. Which adaptation would the coach be counting on?

options.text: A larger plasma volume and maybe more red cells, raising oxygen delivery
options.why: Right: more blood volume and haemoglobin mass would carry more oxygen.

options.text: Sweating that starts at a higher core temperature
options.why: Acclimation lowers the sweat onset threshold; this would also not help cool-air VO₂max.

options.text: A higher skin temperature during hard efforts
options.why: A higher skin temperature is a heat burden, not a benefit.

options.text: Lower muscle blood flow to save oxygen
options.why: Lower muscle blood flow would limit performance.

variants.stem: Which statement about the speed of the two adaptations is right?

options.text: Plasma volume changes within days; haemoglobin mass needs weeks
options.why: Right: plasma volume is fast, and red cell production is slow.

options.text: Both change within two days of the first session
options.why: Red cell production cannot be this fast.

options.text: Haemoglobin mass changes first, plasma volume after weeks
options.why: The order is reversed.

options.text: Neither changes in less than six months
options.why: Plasma volume changed within 10 days in the studies.

variants.stem: In the 2010 trial of heat acclimation, by about how much did VO₂max rise when tested in cool air?

options.text: About 1%
options.why: Too small; the reported gain in cool air was larger.

options.text: About 5%
options.why: Right: 66.8 to 70.2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ in cool conditions.

options.text: About 15%
options.why: Too large for this trial.

options.text: It did not change
options.why: It changed in the heat group; it was the controls who did not change.

variants.stem: The 2010 trial had 12 heat cyclists and 8 matched controls who were not randomised. What does this do to the result?

options.text: It makes the result strong enough to change training advice by itself
options.why: A small, non-randomised study is not enough alone.

options.text: It makes the result weak: small groups and matching leave room for chance and bias
options.why: Right: without random allocation, groups may differ in ways that matter.

options.text: It makes the result invalid because controls were used
options.why: Using controls is a strength; the weakness is size and lack of randomisation.

options.text: It has no effect, since matched groups are the same as randomised ones
options.why: Matching on some traits does not balance the traits that were not matched.

variants.stem: In a cool 15 km time trial, a heat group went from 298 to 315 W and a control group from 294 to 311 W. What did heat training add?

options.why: This credits heat with the whole change of the heat group; the controls gained 17 W too.

options.text: 0 W
options.why: Right: 17 W (heat) − 17 W (control) = 0 W net.
This adds the two changes instead of subtracting them.

options.text: 4 W
options.why: This is the starting gap between the groups (298 − 294), not the effect.

variants.solution: Heat change = 315 − 298 = 17 W. Control change = 311 − 294 = 17 W. Net = 17 − 17 = 0 W.

variants.stem: In a cool time trial, a heat group went from 280 to 300 W and a control group from 282 to 292 W. What did heat training add?

options.why: This credits heat with the whole change of the heat group; controls gained 10 W too.
This adds the two changes instead of subtracting them.
This is the starting gap between the groups, not the effect.

variants.solution: Heat change = 300 − 280 = 20 W. Control change = 292 − 282 = 10 W. Net = 20 − 10 = 10 W.

variants.stem: In a cool time trial, a heat group went from 310 to 325 W and a control group from 308 to 312 W. What did heat training add?

options.why: This credits heat with the whole change of the heat group; controls gained 4 W too.
This adds the two changes instead of subtracting them.
This is the starting gap between the groups, not the effect.

variants.solution: Heat change = 325 − 310 = 15 W. Control change = 312 − 308 = 4 W. Net = 15 − 4 = 11 W.

variants.stem: In a 5.5 week trial, both the heat group and the control group improved a cool time trial by about 17 W. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Ordinary training, practice and season progress improved both groups; heat added no detectable gain
options.why: Right: the control group shows what normal training gave in the same period.

options.text: Heat training works, because the heat group improved
options.why: The control group improved just as much, so the gain cannot be credited to heat.

options.text: The control group must have secretly trained in heat
options.why: Nothing suggests this; the control trained in cool conditions.

options.text: Time trials improve by 17 W for everybody, whatever training they do
options.why: Gains depend on training; here they are explained by what both groups did.

variants.stem: One 2010 trial found a 5% VO₂max gain in cool air after heat training. Three later trials found none. What is the most careful statement?

options.text: The results conflict and designs differ, so no firm cool-air gain can be claimed
options.why: Right: both 'it works' and 'it does not work' overstate what small trials with different designs show.

options.text: The 2010 trial is right, because it came first and set the pattern
options.why: Being first does not make a study right.

options.text: The later trials are right, because they are newer and more careful
options.why: Newer trials are not always better; they are small too.

options.text: The true effect is half of the 2010 result, which is about 2.5%
options.why: Averaging conflicting small trials does not give the true effect.

variants.stem: In a 5.5 week trial, plasma volume rose by 303 mL with heat training and by 188 mL with cool training. What does this suggest?

options.text: Plasma volume expansion is not specific to heat; hard training raises it too
options.why: Right: it rose in both groups, so part of the heat group's rise is a training effect.

options.text: Cool training is better than heat training for plasma volume
options.why: The heat group's rise was larger; the finding is that both rose.

options.text: Plasma volume does not change with training at all
options.why: It rose significantly in both groups.

options.text: The cool group must have been exposed to heat
options.why: The control group trained only in cool conditions.

variants.stem: In 25 elite skiers, heat suit training raised haemoglobin mass by 30 g more than control, but a 15 min running trial and VO₂max did not differ. What is the best reading?

options.text: Haemoglobin mass rose, but a performance benefit is not shown
options.why: Right: the test measured what mattered and found no detectable difference.

options.text: Heat suits are useless and should never be used
options.why: One trial in one group cannot prove they are useless, and haemoglobin mass did rise.

options.text: The performance test must be wrong because haemoglobin mass rose
options.why: A rise in one marker does not mean performance must rise.

options.text: A 30 g rise in haemoglobin mass is large enough to win races
options.why: The data do not show a performance gain at all.

variants.stem: A counterbalanced crossover with 7 men found no change in cool-air performance after heat training. How should you read this null result?

options.text: As weak evidence of no effect: a study this small can miss a small real gain
options.why: Right: the crossover design helps, but 7 people give little power to detect small effects.

options.text: As proof that heat training never works in cool air
options.why: A small null study cannot prove 'never'.

options.text: As proof that heat training works, because plasma volume rose
options.why: Plasma volume rose, yet performance did not change; none of the changes correlated with performance.

options.text: As meaningless, because crossover studies are not valid
options.why: Crossover designs are valid and often efficient; size is the issue.
